title: Restoring Wetlands: The Return of the Beaver

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For roughly four centuries, beavers were absent from the British landscape. Hunted for their dense fur and for castoreum, a secretion used in perfumery and medicine, the animals had been driven to extinction in England and Wales by the sixteenth century, and in Scotland not long afterwards. Their disappearance went largely unremarked, since few people living beside rivers could remember a time when the species had shaped them. It is only in recent decades that ecologists have begun to ask what was lost along with the animal. The answer, according to a growing body of research, is a remarkable amount of natural infrastructure, and several conservation bodies now argue that restoring the beaver may be among the most cost-effective ways of repairing damaged wetlands.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The beaver's influence stems from its habit of building dams. Using branches, stones and mud, a family group blocks a stream to create a pond deep enough to protect its lodge from predators and to keep the entrance permanently underwater. A single dam may be only a metre high, yet a series of them along a valley can transform a narrow channel into a mosaic of pools, side channels and damp meadow. Beavers also fell trees, and the resulting gaps in the canopy let light reach the ground, encouraging a denser growth of sedges and flowering plants. Because the animals repair their structures constantly, the system is never static; ponds shift, drain and refill over the years, producing a changing habitat rather than a fixed one that must be managed by people.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The consequences for water are considerable. A dam slows the passage of a stream, so that rain falling on higher ground is released gradually instead of rushing downstream within hours. Surveys of beaver-occupied catchments have found that the ponds can hold large volumes of water during storms, reducing the height of flood peaks in villages further down the valley. In dry summers the same ponds work in reverse, seeping water back into the channel and sustaining flows when neighbouring streams shrink to a trickle. Sediment is also trapped behind the dams, which means that the water leaving a beaver complex is often markedly clearer than the water entering it, an effect that matters to anyone responsible for drinking supplies and for the cost of treating them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Wildlife benefits as well. The ponds provide breeding sites for amphibians, which need still water to lay their eggs, while the dead and decaying timber attracts insects on which bats and birds feed. Fish gain from the cooler, shaded pools, in which young trout can shelter during hot weather, although some biologists note that dams may obstruct the upstream movement of migrating salmon at certain times of year. On balance, however, the diversity of species recorded around beaver wetlands is consistently higher than in comparable stretches of straightened stream, and several uncommon plants have appeared in clearings that were opened up by felled willow and alder. Such findings help to explain why the beaver is now described as a keystone species, one whose activity supports many others.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Much of the strongest evidence comes from a fenced trial begun in a lowland catchment with a single breeding pair. Before the animals were released, researchers installed gauges to record water levels and collected samples of invertebrates and plants for comparison. Within five years the pair and their offspring had built more than a dozen dams, and the monitoring showed that the peak flow of water leaving the site after heavy rain had fallen by a substantial proportion. The researchers stress, however, that one site cannot settle the question, since the benefits depend on the shape of the valley, the type of soil and the number of animals present.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes the animals. Farmers whose fields lie beside rivers worry about flooded pasture and about burrows weakening banks, while owners of orchards and woodland have seen valuable timber gnawed through. Fishing interests raise concerns about obstructed passage for salmon. Such objections are not trivial, and experience in other European countries suggests that conflict is most likely where land has been drained right to the water's edge. Fortunately, remedies exist. Pipes can be fitted through dams to keep pond levels below an agreed height, and wire mesh around the trunks of prized trees deters gnawing at little expense.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The question for policymakers is therefore not whether beavers should be returned, but where and under what rules. Some advocates favour a licensing system under which landowners could request animals for their own land, while others prefer to let populations spread naturally and to deal with problems as they arise. Both approaches require funding for advisers who can negotiate between neighbours, and both depend on patient monitoring of results. What seems clear is that the beaver, once regarded as a pest or merely as a source of fur, is now being valued for the services it provides free of charge, and that learning to live alongside it may prove considerably cheaper than the concrete defences built to do the same work.
